scenario: Agent1 and Agent2 are friends who enjoy dining out together. They decide to try a new restaurant that is known for its unique dining experience where guests are encouraged to order without looking at the menu. Agent1 is excited about the surprise element, while Agent2 is more hesitant and prefers to make informed choices. Agent1 wants to convince Agent2 to fully embrace the restaurant's concept and order without previewing the menu.
learner_goal: Encourage Agent2 to participate in the spontaneous dining experience without looking at the menu, highlighting the excitement of trying something new. (<extra_info>Extra information: Agent2 usually likes to be in control and may need reassurance that the surprise can be enjoyable.</extra_info>)
evaluation_reasoning:

transcript.speaker: Mia Davis
transcript.content: Come on, William—let’s do the surprise thing tonight. The staff will check allergies and you can tell them any absolute no-go’s, so you’re not locked into something you hate, and if it really flops we can always grab something familiar after. Trust me—I used to thrive on surprises back in my punk days; this will be fun, I promise.

transcript.speaker: William Brown
transcript.content: Okay, I like the idea — but let’s set a couple of guardrails so nobody gets stuck with a dealbreaker. We tell the staff our allergies/absolute no‑gos, do blind ordering for just the starter and dessert (or ask the kitchen to give one‑line hints for each surprise dish), and pick the main from a short revealed list. If anything’s truly awful, we bail to something familiar — sound fair?
